metadata.title: Tangent at a point of a circle: perpendicular to the radius
metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.objective: Show why the tangent at a point on a unit circle is perpendicular to the radius.
metadata.learner: Knows circle geometry and basic sine and cosine.
misconceptions: A tangent is a kind of radius
The perpendicularity is an accident of the point drawn
expectedUnderstanding: P is a point of the unit circle and OP is a radius of length 1.
The tangent is the line through P that meets the circle at P and nowhere else.
At every position of P the angle between OP and the tangent is 90 degrees, so the right angle is a consequence of what a tangent is, not a feature of one drawing.
The reason: the line through P perpendicular to OP is at distance exactly one radius from O, so it cannot cross the circle at a second point.

properties.label: P along the circle (x of P, in radii)

primitives.text: The tangent at a point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius
The tangent meets the circle at P, and only at P.
The angle between OP and the tangent is 90 degrees.
Slide P: both lines turn, the square stays closed.
So the right angle is a rule, not luck of position.
A line through P at right angles to OP stays one radius from O, so it can meet the circle only at P.

checkpoints.title: Predict
checkpoints.body: The blue segment is the radius, the black line is the tangent. Before anything moves: is the angle between them 90 degrees at this particular P only, or at every P?

checkpoints.title: Read the angle
checkpoints.body: P is now at the top of the circle: the radius points straight up and the tangent runs horizontally. What is the angle at P, and which line is doing the turning?

checkpoints.title: Check the move
checkpoints.body: P slid to the far side and both lines turned. Did the red square open or close, and is the tangent still touching the circle at one point only?

checkpoints.title: Push it further
checkpoints.body: If a line through P were not perpendicular to OP, where else would it have to meet the circle? Answer with the distance from O to that line.

narration.text: The circle has centre O and radius 1. The blue segment OP joins the centre to a chosen point P on the circle.
The black line is the tangent at P: it touches the circle at P and meets it nowhere else.
The red square marks the angle where the radius and the tangent meet. Here it is 90 degrees, at this particular P.
Is that luck of position? Slide P and watch: the radius turns, the tangent turns with it, and the red square stays closed.
The reason is a distance. Turn the radius by 90 degrees at P and you get a line that is exactly one radius away from O, so it can reach the circle only at P.
Being the tangent and being perpendicular are the same condition, at every point of the circle. The tangent is a line, not a radius: the radius is the segment from O to P.

fallback.text: Static figure, three positions of P on a unit circle of radius 150 pixels, centre O. Position 1: P at 37 degrees above the horizontal, radius drawn from O to P, tangent drawn through P, and a small red square at P between the two lines. Position 2: P at 90 degrees, the radius vertical and the tangent horizontal, the same red square at P. Position 3: P at 143 degrees, radius and tangent both tilted the other way, the red square still closed. Caption: at each position the tangent touches the circle only at P and meets the radius at 90 degrees, because the line through P perpendicular to OP lies exactly one radius from O and so cannot cross the circle again.

accessibility.alt: A unit circle of radius 1 with centre O. A blue radius runs from O to a point P on the circle, marked with a blue dot and the letter P. A black line passes through P, touches the circle there and extends both ways without crossing the circle again. A small red square sits at P in the corner between the radius and the black line. A slider moves P round the upper part of the circle: as P moves, the radius and the tangent both rotate and the red square stays a square, held at 90 degrees.
